USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture without further escalation, engage actively in the upcoming October talks, and signal willingness to negotiate a deal — but do not roll back tariffs or make concessions before extracting meaningful structural commitments from Beijing. The scheduled Oct 1 hike to 30% on List 3 ($250B) should be used as leverage in the October round, not fired as a punitive measure beforehand.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.3 reflects that the trade war is inflicting real, measurable damage on the US economy — manufacturing is in recession (two consecutive quarters of contraction, only 3,000 manufacturing jobs added in August vs. 22,000/month average in 2018), GDP growth has slowed to ~1.6% (Salon/Moody's, Sep 11), Goldman Sachs estimates a cumulative 0.6% GDP drag and projects Q4 growth at 1.8% (NBC/Goldman, Aug 12), and Moody's estimates 300,000 jobs already lost with 900,000 at risk by end-2020 (Salon, Sep 11). Consumer-facing List 4A tariffs (15% on ~$110-125B, effective Sep 1) are now hitting finished goods, meaning consumers will feel price increases directly (NBC, Aug 12). Public concern is severe: 38% approval (ABC/WaPo poll, Sep 10), 56% disapprove of China trade handling, 6 in 10 Americans expect a recession within a year.

However, the threat is not existential because the US holds significant structural leverage. China's economy is under considerably greater strain: industrial production grew only 4.8% in July — a 17-year low and well below the 5.8% consensus (CNN, Aug 14). China's PPI has turned negative for the first time in three years (Forbes, Aug 9). Manufacturing PMI spent three months in contraction territory this summer (CNN, Sep 2). China's Q2 GDP growth at 6.2% is the weakest since quarterly reporting began in 1992 (WaPo, Sep 18). Beijing is responding with stimulus (900 billion yuan reserve cut, two trillion yuan in tax cuts) but these are defensive measures, not signs of strength.

The action score of -0.05 (borderline hold/negotiate) reflects that the US should stay engaged in talks without making new commitments. The October round of negotiations is the 13th high-level meeting — both sides have agreed to it (Reuters, Sep 5; China commerce ministry confirmed Liu He will travel to Washington). China has already offered modest goodwill gestures: a tariff-exemption list for 16 categories of US products (timeline, Sep 11) and exclusion of soybeans, pork, and some farm goods from additional retaliatory tariffs (timeline, Sep 13). These are signals of a Beijing looking for off-ramps, not escalation.

Escalating further (e.g., raising List 3 to 30% on Oct 1 as threatened, or broadening the entity list) risks tipping the US into recession — a scenario UBS, Moody's, and Goldman Sachs all flag as plausible under further escalation. With the 2020 election cycle beginning, the administration cannot afford to own a recession triggered by its own trade policy. The smarter play is to let the existing tariff pressure continue to bite China's economy while keeping the negotiating channel open, using the Oct 1 scheduled hike as bargaining leverage rather than executing it preemptively. The structural issues (IP theft, forced tech transfer, state subsidies) remain the US's core demands — these can only be resolved at the negotiating table, not through additional unilateral tariffs.
